summary.text: A heat wave is a period of abnormally hot weather lasting several days, usually measured against the area's usual climate and normal temperatures for the season.
Heat waves form when a high-pressure area in the upper atmosphere strengthens and stays over a region, trapping heat near the ground.
Since the 1950s they have become more frequent and intense over land almost everywhere, with climate change driving the rise in frequency and duration.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: A strong high-pressure area lingering overhead

facts.label: High pressure lingers
facts.value: Several days up to several weeks

facts.label: Sweden's definition
facts.value: Five or more days in a row above 25 °C

facts.label: Singapore's threshold
facts.value: Daily highs averaging 35 °C for three days

facts.label: 2024 records
facts.value: Reported in Europe, North America and China

items.prompt: A week of 30 °C days is ordinary in one city but declared a heat wave in another. How can both be right?

options.label: Each place judges heat against its own usual climate
Thermometers read differently in each city
Only coastal cities can have heat waves
One city must have measured it wrongly

items.explain: Heat waves are measured relative to an area's usual climate, so temperatures normal in a hotter place can count as a heat wave in a cooler one.

items.prompt: Weather forecasters spot a pattern that often brings a heat wave. What is it?

options.label: A low-pressure storm stalling nearby
Strong sea breezes blowing inland
A thin, even layer of cloud
A strong high-pressure area parked overhead

items.explain: Heat waves form when an upper-atmosphere high-pressure area strengthens and remains over a region for days or weeks, trapping heat near the surface.

items.prompt: Midway through a long hot spell, a city suffers blackouts. How did the heat contribute?

options.label: Sunlight cut the signals between power stations
It added stress to the electrical grid
Hot air stops electricity flowing in wires
Power plants always shut down above 30 °C

items.explain: Heat waves can put additional stress on electrical grids, potentially causing blackouts or brownouts.

items.prompt: Why does a heat wave pose a danger to human health?

options.label: Hot air holds too little oxygen to breathe
Sunlight thins the blood over several days
Heat and sunlight overwhelm the body's cooling
Heat spreads germs much faster than cold

items.explain: Heat and sunlight can overwhelm thermoregulation, the body's control of its own temperature.

items.prompt: Can officials usually warn the public before a heat wave arrives?

options.label: No, they strike with no warning at all
Only once the first hot day has passed
Only in places that have satellites
Yes, they can usually be forecast ahead

items.explain: It is usually possible to forecast heat waves, letting authorities issue warnings in advance.

items.prompt: Sweden counts a heat wave as at least five days in a row with highs above 25 °C. A Swedish town has four days at 27 °C, then cools off. Was that a heat wave?

options.label: Yes, because 27 °C beats the limit
No, it fell one day short
Yes, any run over three days counts
No, the highs needed to pass 30 °C

items.explain: Sweden's definition needs at least five consecutive days above 25 °C, so four days does not qualify.
